versions.analysis_for_next: Main weakness is neutral recall (52/108): 32 neutral texts went to positive and 24 to negative. Positive over-prediction comes from event promotions and announcements (shows, workshops, meetings, radio broadcasts), sports results stated as facts, questions or plans with an '!', and mild opinions ('may be the best thing', 'more comfortable'). Negative over-prediction comes from headlines or commentary containing negative words (worst, bad reputation, implode) without the author's own distress, and from light self-deprecating or joking complaints (lmao, 'I'm dead', 'not ready', procrastination, sorry for the delay). The fix is to make positive require a clear personal positive feeling, not just upbeat or eventful content, and to make negative require clear personal distress or hostility or a report of serious harm. Joking, hedged or mixed tweets and plain promotions should default to neutral. A few positive cases (condolences with blessings, playful jokes) and some negative ones (sarcastic jabs) are noisy, so I will not chase them much. I will add that prayers or blessings toward people count as positive, and that a clear sarcastic jab at someone counts as negative.

Version 1 overcorrected. Neutral recall rose to 93/108, but positive recall fell from 92 to 50 and negative from 91 to 73, so macro-F1 dropped to 66.7. The annotators label as positive many things v1 pushed to neutral: inviting promotions ('come join/celebrate/support', free stuff, win a car, get tickets), the author's plans to attend concerts, films or events, sports wins and achievements reported as news, hopes and wishes, and light amusement. They label as negative many bad-news headlines (deficit, missile strike, funeral, charges, a phone that may break) and quiet complaints ('going to die', 'not cause I enjoy it', misses, desperation). So the dataset treats the polarity of the content, not only explicit emotion, as sentiment. I will return close to v0, which scored better, and fix its main neutral leaks more narrowly. Questions and speculation with no clear stance stay neutral. Dry factual notices that only give a time and place stay neutral. Hyperbolic self-joking ('lmao', 'I'm dead' meaning amused) stays neutral. Blunt or hedged commentary that mixes good and bad stays neutral. I will drop v1's rule that negative words in a factual report do not count, because bad-event news is mostly negative.

Version 2 (70.2) behaves almost like v0 (71.4): positive and negative recall are high, but neutral recall is only 48/108. Of the gold-neutral texts, 35 went to positive and 25 to negative. Version 1 showed the opposite failure: a strict 'explicit emotion only' rule collapsed positive recall. So I need a middle threshold. Looking at gold neutrals predicted positive: routine event notices (meeting at 6pm, RSVP, register, sign up, radio show at 5pm), mid-match sports updates, plain statements of plans ('I'm going to X on Friday'), news of births or birthdays, mild opinions ('may be the best', 'more comfortable than'), and fan requests. Gold positives that v1 missed had stronger signals: hype with '!!!', 'go check it out', 'win', 'come celebrate', 'can't wait', 'perfect', 'impressed', wins of titles or finals, and hopes. Gold neutrals predicted negative: sports snark and wry commentary (implode, padding numbers, could be worse), news headlines about controversies (apologies, mergers, tirades, corrections), and comic self-complaints (not ready, I'm dead, procrastinating, computer broke, the 'Nooooo' scheduling clash). Gold negatives had real harm (missiles, deficits, bombings, funerals) or a bitter personal tone. I will set graded thresholds. Positive needs strong enthusiasm or a completed big success. Negative needs real harm or sincere distress or hostility. Routine notices, progress updates, controversy reporting, wry sports snark and comic complaints go to neutral. Prayers and blessings count as positive.

Version 3 (70.8) swung back toward neutral. Neutral recall is good at 91/108, but 41 positives and 37 negatives were pulled into neutral. The missed positives carry mild but real personal positivity: hope, praying, fun, perfect, liked, impressed, brilliant, 'let's go', plans to watch or reread something the author enjoys, defending someone, 'should be fun to watch'. The missed negatives carry mild personal negativity: bad mood, ACK, wtf, can't sleep, not in the state of mind, going to die, miss, worse than, insensitive, mocking jabs, political cynicism. So annotators label even mild personal feeling as polar. The neutral texts v0 and v2 over-polarized were mostly third-party content: event notices, sports play-by-play, news headlines about controversies, and wry spectator snark. The best split is by source. If the author voices a personal feeling or opinion, even a mild one, pick its polarity. For impersonal news, notices or updates, pick neutral unless the event is clearly good (title won, celebration) or clearly bad (death, attack, crime, loss, scandal). Hyped promotions with '!' or 'come/get your tickets' lean positive; flat time-and-place notices stay neutral.

Two failure modes keep alternating. Broad polar definitions (v0, v2, v4) give 91-93 recall on positive and negative but only 44-52 on neutral. Strict polar definitions (v1, v3) lift neutral to 91-93 but drop positive or negative recall by 25-40. V4's rule that any personal opinion is polar failed because many gold neutrals are personal but carry no explicit feeling word: plain plans ('I'm going to X Oct 9'), comic self-talk with lol or lmao, spectator snark, hedged political opinions, fan requests. V3's misses, by contrast, almost all had an explicit feeling word: fun, hope, perfect, impressed, brilliant, liked, bad mood, ACK, wtf, can't sleep, going to die, miss. So the most reliable test is whether the author uses an explicit feeling word or emoticon, not whether they are personal or impersonal. I will build v5 around that test. Positive or negative needs an explicit feeling word, emoticon or emphatic hype, or a clearly good or bad event. Flat plans, flat notices, play-by-play and questions are neutral. Laughter markers (lol, lmao, haha, bwahaha) turn a gripe into neutral unless a strong negative word is also present. Wry jokes about athletes and celebrities stay neutral. Prayers and condolences that bless a person count as positive.

V5's explicit-signal rule gave the best result so far (76.1). I will keep its structure and fix the leaks at the edges. Neutral→positive (21): exclamation marks with no feeling word ('!!!' in a request, a ticket sale or a radio notice), passing 'thank you' or <3 inside a request, spam offering free stuff, hedged opinions ('may be the best thing', 'more comfortable than'), and excited play-by-play of a game in progress. Neutral→negative (16): policy or business headlines containing words like 'worst' or 'bad reputation' that are not harm events, comic hyperbole ('I'm dead', 'not ready', 'afraid' with :S), and sports snark ('implode'). Positive→neutral (17): enjoyment carried by words like 'celebrate', 'come support', 'fast forward to' or 'on loop', and completed wins such as reaching a final. I will make these small targeted edits. '!' alone, a passing thanks, sales or spam, and requests are not enough for positive. Hedged comparisons and in-progress sports updates are neutral. Negative-sounding words in policy, business or opinion headlines are neutral unless real harm is reported. Comic hyperbole is neutral. 'Celebrate', 'come support' and eager phrases like 'fast forward to' count as positive. Completed wins stay positive. The core rule is unchanged, so the gains should hold.

V6 is the best so far (77.1), with neutral recall at 85, but positive recall slipped to 80 and negative to 84. Positive→neutral (23) has three main groups. First, hedged praise of the author's own experience ('may be the best film I've seen'), which v6's hedged-opinion rule wrongly neutralized. Second, eager anticipation of the author's own event with no keyword ('standing in Wrigley Field waiting for the band!', 'let's go!', 'for sure going to watch', 'please share!!!' for one's own show). Third, confident praise or defense of someone ('does more for the culture', stood up for X). Negative→neutral (19) is mostly disparagement without a feeling word: belittling comparisons ('just X on steroids'), mocking suggestions about someone's looks, cynical rhetorical questions about politicians or court cases, complaints framed as 'I don't know why they haven't…', and sarcastic labels ('Desperation Day'). I will narrow the hedge rule to comparisons about third parties and politics, so hedged praise of the author's own experience is positive. I will count the author's eager anticipation of their own event or show as positive. I will add belittling, mocking, cynical or complaining remarks to negative even without feeling words, while keeping light wry sports commentary and self-directed comic gripes neutral. Everything else stays the same to protect neutral recall.

V7 is the best so far (79.2). Positive recall recovered to 92 and negative is at 91, but neutral→negative rose to 21. The new disparagement rule pulls in texts annotators see as neutral. Sports snark about a player's performance ('implode', 'padding his numbers', 'could be worse, he could be X') was explicitly meant to be neutral, but the model still reads it as mocking. Headlines that report criticism of a company or politician ('worst offense', 'bad reputation', a correction that ends 'clear as mud') were labelled negative. Gripes softened by laughter ('Bwahahaha') and matter-of-fact mishaps or apologies ('computer is broke so I can't play', 'not ready', procrastination questions) also went negative. Meanwhile, real harm in headlines (a missile strike, a man charged and granted bail) was missed. I will make targeted fixes. In neutral, I will name sports-performance snark, reported criticism in headlines, laughter-softened mockery, and matter-of-fact mishaps or apologies. In negative, I will keep disparagement but specify that it must be the author's own put-down of a person, group or idea, and I will stress that news of attacks, missile strikes and criminal charges is negative even when the wording is flat. Positive stays unchanged.

V8 is the best so far (80.8). Errors are now spread out, and many look like label noise (sarcasm read the opposite way, garbled text). The patterns that still look fixable are these. First, a completed match win that sends a player to a final is still neutral (0.34 positive), although finals reached is listed, so I will make 'X beats Y to reach the final or advance toward a title' explicit. Second, optimistic predictions about a favored player ('good chance of winning the title') were missed, so I will add them to positive. Third, fan-drama exaggerations about oneself ('Nooooo', 'not ready for this album', 'I'm dead', 'afraid :S' about a scary film) still go negative, so I will name these as comic hyperbole. Fourth, hedged judgments about TV shows or candidates ('may be the best thing for the show', 'more real than X') still go positive, so I will widen the hedged-opinion rule to cover shows and public figures. I will keep everything else so the gains hold, and add nothing that would loosen negative or positive recall broadly.

Same content as the rejected version 10, trimmed to fit under 300 words. V9 (82.4) is the best so far, and most remaining errors look like noise. The planned edits are unchanged and low-risk. Wry sports snark (implode, padding numbers, could be worse) goes to neutral. Headlines with judgmental words (worst offense, bad reputation, most disliked) go to neutral. Fan campaigns and requests go to neutral, with 'let's go' kept positive only for the author's own plans. To save words, I removed a few redundant cue words and phrases without changing any rule.
